newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ businesses find easing pleasing - National Bank.
newsitem.headline: NZ businesses find easing pleasing - National Bank.

text.p: Business confidence rebounded in July, breaking the dismal trend seen so far this year, the National Bank of New Zealand said on Thursday.
The Lloyds TSB-owned bank said the trigger for the mood swing appeared to be the easier monetary conditions sanctioned by the Reserve Bank of New Zealand (RBNZ) at the end of June.
Chief economist Brendan O'Donovan said the government's 1997/98 budget could take little credit for the confidence rebound, as it offered little in terms of policy vision or ensuring value for money.
A net three percent of respondents now anticipate general business conditions will deteriorate over the coming year, compared to a net 15 percent in June.

O'Donovan said the RBNZ's June 27 monetary policy statement recognised the weakness of economic activity, factored in a monetary easing profile over the next six months, and still delivered a conservative set of inflation forecasts.
"The business community was clearly well pleased," he said.
Confidence had improved across most sectors, with the exception of retailing. The service sector remained the most optimistic about its own prospects and those of the economy.

Indicators to improve slightly were confidence, activity outlook, investment, capacity utilisation, interest rate and inflation expectations. The only indicators to deteriorate were residential construction intentions and profits.
Pricing intentions remained very weak,indicating no threat to the prospect of easier monetary conditions over the next six months, O'Donovan said.
He said confidence in the domestic sectors tended to be falling while exporters were becoming more upbeat as the New Zealand dollar fell.

Investment intentions remained low, driven by weak sales expectations and receiving little impetus from falling interest rates. Profit expectations had slid further, with a net five percent of respondents expecting a decline in real profits over the next 12 months.
Export intentions remained strong, with a net 23 percent of respondents expecting to increase exports.
Inflation expectations edged down to 2.5 percent from 2.6 percent in June.

A net 16 percent of respondents expect interest rates to decline over the next 12 months, which O'Donovan said was consistent with the RBNZ's monetary policy stance. It was not clear how much of the easing would occur via the exchange rate rather than interest rates, however.
